positions/orthodox-oikonomia-remarriage/: Orthodox oikonomia and penitential remarriage
Economy in marriage
Second and third marriages
Ecclesiastical divorce

Marriage is a holy mystery meant to be eternal, but when it has spiritually died the Church may, by pastoral economy (oikonomia), grant a divorce and allow a second or even third marriage with a penitential rite.
Christian marriage is unique and ideally eternal, even beyond death (hence a sober rite for second marriages).
Adultery and other grave causes can destroy the marriage; the Church recognises this death rather than declaring the marriage never existed.
Oikonomia is the Church’s merciful application of canons for salvation.
No more than three marriages are permitted (Tome of Union, 920).
Matthew 5:32; 19:9
1 Corinthians 7:15
Basil, Canonical Letters 188, 199, 217 (canons 4, 9, 48, 77, 80)

Grounded in Matthew’s exception and in Basil of Caesarea’s canons (c.374–375); Byzantine imperial law permitted divorce on several grounds; the Tome of Union (920) ended a dispute over Emperor Leo VI’s fourth marriage by limiting marriages to three.
Theodore the Studite (as rigorist critic)
John Meyendorff
Patriarch Nicholas Mystikos
Matthew’s exception explicitly allows divorce for porneia.
It combines a high ideal with realistic mercy for human failure.
It honours the reality of a marriage that existed instead of retroactively denying it (as annulment does).
Catholics argue it contradicts Jesus’ unqualified prohibition in Mark and Luke and Paul’s "let her remain unmarried".
Critics note that Byzantine practice was influenced by imperial law rather than theology.
Some Protestants find the limit of three marriages arbitrary.
Orthodox answer that economy does not deny the ideal but applies it pastorally, as the Church always has.
They point out that Trent deliberately worded its canon so as not to condemn Eastern practice.

positions/erasmian-divorce/name: Erasmian view of divorce and remarriage (Protestant)
positions/erasmian-divorce/oneLine: Marriage is meant to be lifelong, but Scripture permits divorce with freedom to remarry for adultery (Matthew’s exception) and wilful desertion (1 Corinthians 7:15), and many add abuse as a form of desertion.
positions/erasmian-divorce/coreClaims/0: Jesus’ "except it be for fornication" (Matt 5:32; 19:9) allows the innocent party to divorce and remarry.
positions/erasmian-divorce/coreClaims/1: Paul’s "a brother or a sister is not under bondage" (1 Cor 7:15) frees the deserted spouse.
positions/erasmian-divorce/coreClaims/2: Divorce, where allowed, dissolves the marriage so that remarriage is not adultery.
positions/erasmian-divorce/coreClaims/3: Reconciliation should be sought where possible.
positions/erasmian-divorce/origin: Erasmus’s annotations on 1 Corinthians 7 (1519) argued for divorce and remarriage; adopted by Luther, Bucer, Calvin, Beza (On Divorce, 1569) and Protestant marriage courts; confessed in the Westminster Confession (1647); modern scholars such as David Instone-Brewer add neglect and abuse based on Exodus 21:10–11.
positions/erasmian-divorce/strongestArgu: It takes Matthew’s exception and Paul’s desertion clause at face value.
In Jewish context a divorce certificate always conferred the right to remarry.
It protects innocent victims of adultery, desertion and abuse.
positions/erasmian-divorce/strongestObje: Catholics and permanence-view evangelicals argue that Mark, Luke and Paul’s "remain unmarried" exclude remarriage.
Critics note that Protestant societies moved from limited grounds to no-fault divorce, suggesting a slippery slope.
positions/erasmian-divorce/responses/0: Advocates answer that the problem with no-fault divorce is its departure from biblical grounds, not the grounds themselves.
positions/erasmian-divorce/responses/1: They argue that Matthew’s exception was preserved precisely to clarify the shorter sayings.
positions/erasmian-divorce/consequences/: Protestant civil divorce laws from the 16th century.
Mainstream evangelical and mainline pastoral practice.
positions/permanence-view/name: Permanence view (no remarriage while a spouse lives)
positions/permanence-view/altNames/1: Early church view (as claimed by advocates)
positions/permanence-view/oneLine: Separation, and in some cases legal divorce, may be permitted, but remarriage while the former spouse is alive is adultery, because the one-flesh covenant lasts until death.
positions/permanence-view/coreClaims/0: "Whosoever putteth away his wife, and marrieth another, committeth adultery" (Mark 10:11; Luke 16:18).
positions/permanence-view/coreClaims/1: Paul: "let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled" (1 Cor 7:11); a wife is bound "as long as her husband liveth" (Rom 7:2; 1 Cor 7:39).
positions/permanence-view/coreClaims/2: Matthew’s exception refers to betrothal unfaithfulness or unlawful unions, not to consummated marriages.
positions/permanence-view/coreClaims/3: Covenant faithfulness mirrors God’s faithfulness to his unfaithful people (Hosea).
positions/permanence-view/origin: Many early Christian writers (Hermas, Justin, Clement of Alexandria, Jerome) forbade remarriage after divorce; maintained in Catholic doctrine (with annulment) and revived among some evangelicals (William Heth and Gordon Wenham, Jesus and Divorce, 1984; John Piper).
positions/permanence-view/strongestArgum: The shorter and arguably earlier sayings in Mark and Luke have no exception.
The disciples’ shocked reaction (Matt 19:10) suggests Jesus taught something stricter than the rabbinic options.
positions/permanence-view/strongestObjec: Most Protestants and the Orthodox read Matthew’s exception and 1 Corinthians 7:15 as permitting remarriage.
It may leave abandoned or abused spouses without the possibility of a new marriage, which critics see as unjust.
The betrothal interpretation of "porneia" is contested.
positions/permanence-view/responses/0: Advocates answer that celibacy is a calling empowered by grace and that the church must support the abandoned.
positions/permanence-view/responses/1: They argue that hard teaching is not unjust if it reflects Christ’s word and God’s faithfulness.
positions/permanence-view/consequences/0: Minority practice in some evangelical, Anabaptist and Reformed churches.
positions/permanence-view/consequences/1: Restrictions on remarried members in certain plain churches.
positions/contraception-natural-law/oneL: The unitive and procreative meanings of the marital act are inseparable by God’s design, so deliberately rendering intercourse infertile is morally wrong, though spouses may space births for serious reasons by using natural infertile periods.
positions/contraception-natural-law/core: Each marital act must remain open to the transmission of life (Humanae Vitae 11).
Natural law, known by reason, reveals the meaning of human sexuality.
Periodic abstinence respects the body’s rhythms; artificial contraception overrides them.
Separating sex from procreation tends to degrade marriage, women and social morality (HV 17).
Responsible parenthood is a real duty, exercised within these limits.
positions/contraception-natural-law/orig: The early and medieval church condemned contraceptive potions and practices (Augustine, Jerome; canon law); all major churches opposed contraception until Lambeth 1930. Pius XI (Casti Connubii, 1930), Pius XII (1951, permitting rhythm), Paul VI (Humanae Vitae, 1968) and John Paul II (Theology of the Body, 1979–84) formed modern Catholic teaching.
positions/contraception-natural-law/stro: It was the unanimous Christian teaching for nineteen centuries.
Paul VI’s predictions about the effects of widespread contraception on sexual mores are often said to have been vindicated.
It integrates body and person, avoiding a technological approach to sexuality.
Most Protestants and many Catholic theologians argue that the distinction between natural and artificial methods is morally thin when the intention to avoid conception is the same.
The papal commission’s majority (1966) and many lay Catholics believed responsible parenthood can justify contraception.
Critics note its burden on women and the poor, and its non-reception among most Western Catholics.
positions/contraception-natural-law/resp: Defenders answer that the moral difference lies in the act itself: abstaining is not the same as rendering an act infertile.
They point to the growing literature on natural family planning’s effectiveness and to support for the teaching in Africa and among younger Catholics.
positions/contraception-natural-law/cons: A major point of dissent and authority crisis in post-1968 Catholicism.
John Paul II’s Theology of the Body.
positions/contraception-responsible-pare: Contraception permitted for responsible parenthood
Lambeth 1930 view
Family planning
Responsible parenthood (Protestant)

Within marriage, couples may use contraception to plan or limit their families for morally sound reasons, since sexual union has a God-given unitive purpose that is not limited to procreation in every act.
Marital love and companionship are goods in their own right (1 Cor 7:3–5; Song of Songs).
God calls couples to responsible stewardship of procreation, considering health, economics and vocation.
The moral relevance lies in the couple’s overall openness to children and motives, not each act.
Methods that do not destroy an embryo are acceptable; abortifacient methods raise separate concerns.

Lambeth Conference Resolution 15 (1930), followed by the US Federal Council of Churches (1931) and most Protestant churches by the 1960s; also the majority report of the Pontifical Commission on Birth Control (1966). Many Orthodox theologians accept non-abortifacient contraception within marriage by pastoral guidance.

Scripture never explicitly condemns contraception; the Onan story concerns refusal of levirate duty.
Couples using natural family planning share the same intention of avoiding conception.
It allows families to care for children, maternal health and limited resources responsibly.
Catholics argue it severs sex from procreation and opened the way to the sexual revolution.
Critics note that Lambeth’s cautious permission rapidly became universal acceptance.
Some Protestant pro-natalists ("quiverfull") argue children are an unqualified blessing to be welcomed without limit.
Advocates reply that the sexual revolution has many causes and that Christian ethics can affirm contraception within marriage alone.
They argue that responsible stewardship, not maximal fertility, honours God’s gift of children.

positions/complementarianism/oneLine: Men and women are equal in dignity and value as God’s image-bearers, but God has assigned them distinct, complementary roles: loving male headship in marriage and male leadership in the eldership or pastorate of the church.
positions/complementarianism/coreClaims/: Equality of essence and distinction of role are compatible (as in the Trinity, some argue, though this analogy is disputed among complementarians).
Headship is rooted in creation order before the fall (1 Tim 2:13; 1 Cor 11:8–9), not in culture.
Husbands are to love sacrificially; wives to submit respectfully (Eph 5:22–33).
Women may exercise many ministries, but the office of elder/pastor is reserved to qualified men.
positions/complementarianism/origin: Male headship was the general assumption of historic Christian teaching; the term "complementarian" arose in response to evangelical feminism with the Danvers Statement (1987) of the Council on Biblical Manhood and Womanhood and Recovering Biblical Manhood and Womanhood (1991). Catholic and Orthodox churches hold a related but distinct sacramental basis for a male priesthood.
positions/complementarianism/strongestAr: Paul grounds his instructions in creation (1 Tim 2:13), not merely in local circumstances.
Jesus chose twelve male apostles despite countercultural treatment of women.
The church’s consistent practice for nearly two millennia supports it.
positions/complementarianism/strongestOb: Egalitarians argue the key texts address specific local problems (e.g. false teaching in Ephesus) and that Galatians 3:28 sets the trajectory.
Critics note that complementarian cultures have sometimes enabled abuse and suppressed women’s gifts.
Appeals to the "eternal subordination" of the Son provoked a major intra-evangelical controversy in 2016 over orthodoxy on the Trinity.
positions/complementarianism/responses/0: Complementarians answer that abuse violates, not expresses, biblical headship, which is modelled on Christ’s self-giving love.
positions/complementarianism/responses/1: Many have distanced themselves from eternal-subordination arguments while retaining creation-order exegesis.
positions/complementarianism/consequence: Southern Baptist Baptist Faith and Message (2000) restricts pastorate to men.
Shapes the Presbyterian Church in America, many Pentecostal and non-denominational churches.
Ongoing debates on women preaching (e.g. SBC 2023).
